output:
Following the death of Theodora, Antonina and her husband lost imperial favor, experiencing a decline in their later years similar to the misfortunes of the Marlboroughs [p. 101]. 

The year 532, which marked the end of the Persian War, also saw the emergence of a significant threat to the Emperor’s power: the "Blues" and "Greens" [p. 101]. While these groups originated as circus factions, the author notes they had grown into political parties that interfered in politics and religious controversies [p. 101]. In 530, being a "Green" implied being a Monophysite and a partisan of the late Emperor Anastasius, whereas the "Blues" posed as orthodox partisans of the house of Justinus [p. 101]. The author characterizes these groups as being dominated by "rougher elements" prone to "riot and mischief," describing them as a "serious danger to the State" [p. 101].

In January 532, serious rioting broke out. Although Justinian typically favored the Blues, he ordered the execution of leaders from both factions [p. 101]. After four rioters were beheaded before a mob, an attempt to hang three others failed twice due to the bungling of the executioners and the menaces of the crowd; the criminals eventually sought sanctuary in a monastery [p. 102].

This incident triggered six days of desperate rioting. The Blues and Greens united under the watchword "Nika" ("conquer") to demand the deposition of the finance minister, John of Cappadocia, and the city prefect, Eudemius [p. 102]. The author describes Justinian as being "weak enough" to promise the dismissal of these officials, but the mob remained uncontrollable [p. 102]. The unrest was further fomented by partisans of the late emperor who sought to replace Justinian with Hypatius, the nephew of Anastasius [p. 102]. At this time, the city was nearly devoid of troops because the garrison had been deployed to the Persian War, leaving the Emperor with only 4,000 Imperial Guards, some German auxiliaries, and a regiment [p. 102].
